t: Why fsspec-rs uses explicit protocols and shared traits
x: Why fsspec-rs uses explicit protocols and shared traits fsspec-rs has two integration boundaries: Python’s fsspec interface and a reusable Rust filesystem trait. Keeping both boundaries explains the package’s protocol names, backend structure, and separate Python bridge crate. Explicit protocols preserve compatibility fsspec already assigns file, local, and s3 to established Python implementations. Replacing those registrations globally would make importing fsspec-rs change unrelated application behavior. The file-rs, local-rs, and s3-rs names make backend selection visible in configuration and allow both implementations to coexist. The classes still inherit from fsspec.spec.AbstractFileSystem. Code written against fsspec operations can therefore select a Rust backend without adopting a separate Python API. The file-rs, local-rs, and s3-rs names make backend selection visible in configuration and allow both implementations to coexist. The classes still inherit from fsspec.spec.AbstractFileSystem. t: Why fsspec-rs uses explicit protocols and shared traits
s: Default methods keep native backends small
x: The Rust FileSystem trait follows fsspec’s template-method shape. A backend implements primitive operations such as listing, metadata, open, copy, and removal. Default trait methods build higher-level operations such as walking, recursive removal, and local transfers from those primitives. This design centralizes shared path and traversal behavior while leaving storage-specific I/O in LocalFs and S3Fs. The trade-off is that a default method may not exploit every backend-specific optimization; a backend can override behavior when that distinction matters.

t: Why fsspec-rs uses explicit protocols and shared traits
s: The Python bridge is deliberately separate
x: Native Rust backends are not the only filesystems in the fsspec ecosystem. The fsspec_rs_bridge crate adapts an installed Python filesystem to the same Rust trait, so a Rust component running inside Python can consume protocols that have no native Rust implementation. The bridge depends on PyO3 and a Python runtime, while the core fsspec_rs crate does not. Separating them keeps standalone Rust consumers Python-free and makes the runtime cost of crossing into Python explicit. Native backends remain preferable when they exist; the bridge prioritizes ecosystem coverage.

t: Why fsspec-rs uses explicit protocols and shared traits
s: Synchronous semantics form the current common boundary
x: The shipped local and S3 backends implement the synchronous FileSystem trait. S3 uses an internal Tokio runtime to present that interface even though object-store calls are asynchronous underneath. This matches Python file objects and fsspec’s common synchronous surface, at the cost of hiding async scheduling from callers. An experimental AsyncFileSystem trait records a future direction without changing the synchronous contract. Its status and exact trait methods are documented in the Rust reference.

fsspec-rs filesystems fsspec-rs exposes Rust-backed filesystems through normal fsspec classes. Importing fsspec_rs registers the protocols with fsspec: Filesystem Protocols Class Local filesystem file-rs, local-rs fsspec_rs.LocalFileSystem Amazon S3 s3-rs fsspec_rs.S3FileSystem The standard file, local, and s3 registrations remain unchanged. import fsspec import fsspec_rs with fsspec.open("file-rs:///tmp/example.txt", "rb") as f: data = f.read() Local filesystem LocalFileSystem wraps the Rust LocalFs backend, which uses std::fs for local paths. It is marked as a local filesystem (local_file = True) and supports the common fsspec primitives. from fsspec_rs import LocalFileSystem fs = LocalFileSystem(auto_mkdir=True) fs.pipe_file("/tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt", b"hello") assert fs.exists("/tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt") assert fs.isfile("/tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt") print(fs.info("/tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt")) Paths Direct method calls use normal local paths: fs.cat_file("/tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt") fsspec URLs use file-rs:// or local-rs://: with fsspec.open("local-rs:///tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt", "rb") as f: print(f.read()) LocalFileSystem._strip_protocol() removes only the Rust-specif

LocalFileSystem wraps the Rust LocalFs backend, which uses std::fs for local paths. It is marked as a local filesystem (local_file = True) and supports the common fsspec primitives. from fsspec_rs import LocalFileSystem fs = LocalFileSystem(auto_mkdir=True) fs.pipe_file("/tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt", b"hello") assert fs.exists("/tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt") assert fs.isfile("/tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt") print(fs.info("/tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt"))

Direct method calls use normal local paths: fs.cat_file("/tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt") fsspec URLs use file-rs:// or local-rs://: with fsspec.open("local-rs:///tmp/fsspec-rs/example.txt", "rb") as f: print(f.read()) LocalFileSystem._strip_protocol() removes only the Rust-specific local protocols. The regular file:// and local:// protocols remain owned by fsspec’s Python implementation.

Supported modes are rb, wb, ab, and xb, plus their textless aliases r, w, a, and x at the Rust layer. Python wrappers expose binary file objects that implement read, write, seek, tell, flush, close, readable, writable, and seekable. with fs.open("/tmp/fsspec-rs/out.bin", "wb") as f: f.write(b"payload") with fs.open("/tmp/fsspec-rs/out.bin", "rb") as f: f.seek(2) print(f.read()) auto_mkdir=True creates missing parent directories for write, append, exclusive-create, and copy operations. With the default auto_mkdir=False, missing parents are reported by the operating system.

Local filesystem methods delegated to Rust include: Listing and metadata: ls, info, exists, isdir, isfile, size Reads and writes: open, cat_file, pipe_file, head, tail, read_text, write_text, touch Directory operations: mkdir, makedirs, rmdir, walk, find, du Mutation and transfer: rm_file, rm, cp_file, copy, mv, get_file, put_file The cache_type, block_size, and max_blocks options are accepted by open() for API compatibility. Local reads are already direct local file operations, so those cache options do not change local read behavior.

S3FileSystem wraps the Rust S3Fs backend, which uses Apache Arrow’s object_store crate and runs its async S3 calls through an embedded Tokio runtime. The Python protocol is s3-rs, so it can coexist with s3fs. from fsspec_rs import S3FileSystem fs = S3FileSystem(bucket="my-bucket", region="us-east-1") fs.pipe_file("reports/hello.txt", b"hello") print(fs.cat_file("reports/hello.txt"))

S3FileSystem is constructed for one bucket. Method calls can use keys within that bucket: fs.ls("reports") fs.info("reports/hello.txt") fsspec URLs include the bucket and can infer constructor options through _get_kwargs_from_urls(): with fsspec.open( "s3-rs://my-bucket/reports/hello.txt", "rb", region="us-east-1", ) as f: print(f.read()) Internally, object names are normalized without a leading slash. Directory entries are S3 prefixes, not real directories; mkdir() and rmdir() are no-ops.

Credential resolution follows this order: Explicit constructor arguments: key, secret, token, region, endpoint_url, and anon fsspec.config.conf["s3"], including values populated from fsspec config environment variables object_store’s own AWS credential chain, such as environment variables, profiles, and instance or task roles client_kwargs={"endpoint_url": ...} is accepted for s3fs-compatible configuration. If the endpoint starts with http://, the Rust backend allows plain HTTP automatically for local S3-compatible services. fs = S3FileSystem( bucket="benchmark", key="minioadmin", secret="minioadmin", endpoint_url="http://localhost:9000", region="us-east-1", ) Anonymous access is available with anon=True.

S3 reads support optional Rust-side cache strategies through cache_type: cache_type Behavior none Fetch each requested byte range directly. readahead Keep one lookahead window for sequential reads. block Cache fixed-size blocks with LRU eviction. all Fetch the whole object on first read. with fs.open( "large/table.parquet", "rb", cache_type="block", block_size=8 * 1024 * 1024, ) as f: header = f.read(4096) block_size defaults to 4 MiB. The Rust max_blocks default is 32. The Python file wrapper does not forward max_blocks from open(), so it cannot be configured through that call. Without an explicit cache_type, S3 read mode eagerly loads the whole object into memory. Explicit readahead, block, and none select range-based reads.

S3 methods delegated to Rust include: Listing and metadata: ls, info, exists, isdir, isfile, size Reads and writes: open, cat_file, pipe_file, head, tail, read_text Prefix traversal: walk, find Object mutation: rm_file, rm, cp_file Current S3 writes buffer object contents in memory before upload. Multipart concurrent uploads and signed URLs are not yet part of the public API.

How to use Rust-backed filesystems Use these recipes when replacing a local or S3 filesystem with its fsspec-rs equivalent. Select a backend by protocol Construct filesystems through fsspec when an application accepts a protocol: import fsspec import fsspec_rs local = fsspec.filesystem("file-rs", auto_mkdir=True) s3 = fsspec.filesystem("s3-rs", bucket="reports", region="us-east-1") Use direct classes when an application accepts an AbstractFileSystem instance: from fsspec_rs import LocalFileSystem, S3FileSystem local = LocalFileSystem(auto_mkdir=True) s3 = S3FileSystem(bucket="reports", region="us-east-1") Use fsspec URLs Import fsspec_rs before resolving a protocol in environments that do not discover package entry points automatically: import fsspec import fsspec_rs with fsspec.open("file-rs:///tmp/report.txt", "wb") as file: file.write(b"complete\n") with fsspec.open( "s3-rs://reports/2026/summary.txt", "rb", region="us-east-1", ) as file: summary = file.read() Keep file, local, and s3 URLs when you want the existing Python implementations. Use the -rs protocols to select the Rust-backed implementations explicitly.

Pass the endpoint and credentials accepted by S3FileSystem: from fsspec_rs import S3FileSystem fs = S3FileSystem( bucket="warehouse", endpoint_url="http://localhost:9000", region="us-east-1", key="minioadmin", secret="minioadmin", ) Use anon=True for anonymous access. For AWS, omit explicit credentials to use the credential chain provided by the underlying object-store implementation.

Choose an explicit cache strategy when opening large objects. Omitting cache_type eagerly reads the whole S3 object: with fs.open( "tables/orders.parquet", "rb", cache_type="block", block_size=8 * 1024 * 1024, ) as file: header = file.read(64 * 1024) The Python wrapper uses the Rust default of 32 cached blocks; it does not forward max_blocks. Use none for direct range fetches, readahead for sequential access, block for repeated random access, or all to fetch the complete object on first read. See the filesystem reference for exact behavior and supported operations.

How to build from source Source builds require Rust, hatch-rs 0.4.3 or newer, and the Cargo license collector. From a source checkout, install the collector before installing the Python package: cargo install cargo-bundle-licenses --version 4.2.0 --locked python -m pip install . For an editable development install, use: python -m pip install -e '.[develop]' If collection reports missing license texts, check the versioned overrides and source review requirements. See License bundle reference for the wheel bundle’s coverage.

License bundle reference Wheels include original Cargo dependency license texts in fsspec_rs/licenses/cargo.json. The collector includes dependencies for other targets, so the bundle is a superset of the wheel’s runtime dependencies. Python dependencies, native-library notices, and repaired-wheel libraries are outside its scope. The collector cannot find the r-efi notices in its AUTHORS files. Rust traits and types The fsspec_rs crate is independent of Python. The fsspec_rs_bridge crate adapts Python fsspec objects to its synchronous filesystem trait. Core model Most public Rust types are re-exported from the crate root: use fsspec_rs::{ CacheType, FileInfo, FileSystem, FsFile, FsResult, LocalFs, OpenMode, OpenOptions, S3Config, S3Fs, }; The main pieces are: Type Purpose FileSystem Synchronous filesystem trait with primitive methods and default helpers. Most public Rust types are re-exported from the crate root: use fsspec_rs::{ CacheType, FileInfo, FileSystem, FsFile, FsResult, LocalFs, OpenMode, OpenOptions, S3Config, S3Fs, }; The main pieces are: Type Purpose FileSystem Synchronous filesystem trait with primitive methods and default helpers. AsyncFileSystem Experimental async mirror of FileSystem; no shipped backend implements it yet. FsFile File-like trait returned by FileSystem::open(). FileInfo Metadata for files, directories, and other entries. OpenMode and OpenOptions Open mode and buffered I/O options. FsError and FsResult<T> Shared error and result types. Cache and CacheType Read cache strategy interface and selector.

FileSystem is the sync trait implemented by LocalFs and S3Fs. Required backend methods are seven primitives plus protocol: use fsspec_rs::{FileInfo, FileSystem, FsFile, FsResult, OpenMode, OpenOptions}; struct MyFs; impl FileSystem for MyFs { fn protocol(&self) -> &[&str] { &["myfs"] } fn ls(&self, path: &str, detail: bool) -> FsResult<Vec<FileInfo>> { todo!() } fn rm_file(&self, path: &str) -> FsResult<()> { todo!() } fn cp_file(&self, src: &str, dst: &str) -> FsResult<()> { todo!() } fn open( &self, path: &str, mode: OpenMode, opts: Option<OpenOptions>, ) -> FsResult<Box<dyn FsFile>> { todo!() } fn info(&self, path: &str) -> FsResult<FileInfo> { todo!() } fn mkdir(&self, path: &str, create_parents: bool) -> FsResult<()> { todo!() } fn rmdir(&self, path: &str) -> FsResult<()> { todo!() } } root_marker() defaults to "" and sep() defaults to "/". Backends can override them for local or platform-specific behavior. strip_protocol() and unstrip_protocol() also have defaults and can be overridden when a backend needs bucket-aware or authority-aware paths. The default methods built on those primitives include: Path helpers: strip_protocol, unstrip_protocol, parent Metadata checks: exists

AsyncFileSystem mirrors FileSystem, but primitive methods return futures and default helpers are async fns. It is experimental: the shipped LocalFs and S3Fs backends currently implement the synchronous FileSystem trait. The default async implementation avoids recursive async futures in walk() by using an explicit stack. Method semantics otherwise match FileSystem.
Opened files implement FsFile: FsFile requires Read + Write + Seek + Send. commit() and discard() default to no-ops and are available for buffered writes or future transaction support.

FileInfo is the common metadata value. It stores: name: full path or backend path size: bytes, usually 0 for directories file_type: FileType::File, FileType::Directory, or FileType::Other created and modified: optional SystemTime values extra: backend-specific string metadata such as S3 ETags Convenience constructors are available: let file = FileInfo::file("/tmp/data.bin", 1024); let dir = FileInfo::directory("/tmp"); OpenMode::from_str_mode() accepts rb, wb, ab, xb, and the equivalent single-letter forms. OpenOptions::default() uses a 4 MiB block size, autocommit = true, no explicit cache strategy, and max_blocks = 32.

LocalFs uses std::fs and implements FileSystem. LocalFs::new() starts with auto_mkdir = false. LocalFs::with_auto_mkdir(true) creates missing parent directories during write, append, exclusive-create, and copy operations.

S3Fs wraps object_store::aws::AmazonS3 and presents a sync FileSystem API through an embedded Tokio runtime. S3Config supports: bucket region endpoint_url access_key_id secret_access_key session_token anon virtual_hosted_style_request Plain HTTP is allowed automatically when endpoint_url starts with http://, which is useful for MinIO and LocalStack.

fsspec_rs_bridge exports PyFsspecFs, url_to_fs, and StorageOptions. It is an rlib using PyO3 and Python fsspec at runtime, with no #[pyclass] exports. url_to_fs(url, options) returns a filesystem adapter and start path. PyFsspecFs::from_protocol(protocol, options) constructs an adapter by protocol. Its trait protocol is python; source_protocol() reports the wrapped protocol. The bridge initializes and attaches to the Python interpreter internally. PyFsspecFs implements FileSystem and delegates ls, info, open, cat_file, pipe_file, cp_file, rm_file, mkdir, rmdir, get_file, and put_file to Python. Common Python exceptions map to FsError categories. StorageOptions values support nulls, booleans, signed and unsigned integers, floats, strings, lists, and nested maps. Per-protocol maps configure chained URLs. The Rust guide includes dependency and invocation examples.

The caching layer is used by buffered reads. CacheType::from_str() accepts: Value Strategy none NoCache: every fetch goes to the backend. readahead or read_ahead ReadAheadCache: one lookahead window. block or blockcache BlockCache: fixed-size blocks with LRU eviction. all or bytes AllBytesCache: whole-file cache on first read. Each cache wraps a Fetcher, a FnMut(u64, u64) -> FsResult<Vec<u8>> that retrieves the half-open byte range [start, end) from the backend.

All trait methods return FsResult<T> = Result<T, FsError>. FsError maps common filesystem semantics into stable variants: NotFound PermissionDenied AlreadyExists NotADirectory IsADirectory IoError InvalidArgument NotSupported Other The PyO3 layer maps those variants to Python exceptions such as FileNotFoundError, PermissionError, FileExistsError, NotADirectoryError, IsADirectoryError, ValueError, NotImplementedError, and OSError.

fsspec-rs Use Rust-backed local and S3 filesystems through fsspec. Build Status codecov License PyPI fsspec-rs provides Python classes that inherit from fsspec.AbstractFileSystem and delegate core I/O to Rust. Its native Rust crate exposes shared filesystem traits, local and S3 backends, and read caches. A separate bridge crate adapts Python fsspec implementations for Rust callers. Documentation Read and write a local file walks through the Python API. Use Rust-backed filesystems covers backend selection, S3 endpoints, and caching. Use the Rust crates covers native and Python-backed Rust access. Look up filesystem behavior, Rust traits and types, or the Python API. Read Why fsspec-rs uses explicit protocols and shared traits for the design. For source installations, follow How to build from source. Cargo license overrides The hatch-rs build hook uses license-overrides.json to fill license texts that cargo-bundle-licenses 4.2.0 cannot discover. The file contains only r-efi 5.3.0 and 6.0.0, matched by package name, version, and license identifier. Other dependencies are collected from their source distributions at build time. These overrides require human review before shipping. They do not certify license compliance or change the crates’ declared license choices. Sources Both versions declare MIT OR Apache-2.0 OR LGPL-2.1-or-later. Their AUTHORS files contain the MIT permission text, Apache and LGPL notices, copyright holders, and contributor lists: r-efi 5.3.0 AUTHORS, SHA-256 ff92bed461f50338dd703a9ba9aee496a425957873df1d91192776e4bdf5dda7. r-efi 6.0.0 AUTHORS, SHA-256 d027e91dbc9cdbb2f1190068e498bd6b61cff022b6a032b191021ba658d96111. Each override preserves its version’s complete AUTHORS text. The MIT entry uses that text unchanged. The Apache entry appends the full Apache 2.0 text from the repository’s LICENSE.
